## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator between
real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field, with Hilbert-space
Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger:D(K^\dagger)\to X$. Suppose $K^\dagger$ is
discontinuous on $D(K^\dagger)$ with its norm inherited from $Y$. Let
$(R_\alpha)_{\alpha>0}$ be maps $Y\to X$ such that
$R_\alpha y\to K^\dagger y$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ as
$\alpha\downarrow0$, and let $\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$ be a deterministic
noise-level-free rule. For each exact datum $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ and
$\delta>0$, set $E_y(\delta):=\sup\{\|R_{\alpha(z)}z-K^\dagger y\|_X:z\in Y,\ \|z-y\|_Y\le\delta\}$.
If $E_y(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
then $K^\dagger$ is continuous on $D(K^\dagger).$ Thus, when $K^\dagger$ is
discontinuous, no such noise-level-free rule yields worst-case convergence
over each exact datum's full admissible error balls. The limit is required
separately for each exact datum, not uniformly over $y$. This veto does not
exclude convergence on restricted solution or error classes, stochastic noise
models, or finite-dimensional problems.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert inverse model]]

[[def-ip-unbounded-hilbert-moore-penrose-inverse|Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse and its domain]]

[[def-ip-noise-level-free-parameter-rule|Noise-level-free parameter-choice rule]]

[Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Theorem 4.8](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Sherry, Inverse Problems: Lecture Notes 2024, Theorem 3.12](https://ferdiasherry.com/LectureNotes2024.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a compact linear map $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field, its Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ discontinuous on $D(K^\dagger)$, a family $(R_\alpha)_{\alpha>0}$ that converges pointwise to $K^\dagger$ on this domain, a noise-level-free rule $\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$, and the convergence condition $E_y(\delta)\to0$ for each $y\in D(K^\dagger)$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: For every family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets indexed by $\mathbb N$, there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb N$ such that $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$.

[F1] [[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model]]: The compact inverse model has real or complex Hilbert parameter and data spaces over one scalar field and a compact linear forward map $K:X\to Y$.

[F2] [[def-ip-unbounded-hilbert-moore-penrose-inverse]]: The inverse has domain $D(K^\dagger)=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$ and maps $r+z$ to the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$.

[F3] [[def-ip-noise-level-free-parameter-rule]]: For the fixed operator and reconstruction family, $\alpha$ is a function of the observed datum alone; its value does not take the exact datum or noise bound as input.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ and put $T(y):=R_{\alpha(y)}y$. By [F3], this vector is independent of $\delta$. ## Statement

Under the inputs and instructions of the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson
algorithm, for every $\beta\in[0,1]$ its proposal rule is a Borel probability
kernel and its accept-reject transition $P_\beta$ is a Borel probability
kernel on $H$.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson|The proposal and accept-reject instructions, including the extended potential convention.]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|A probability kernel has probability-measure rows and measurable event evaluations.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The inputs of [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]], a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$, the proposal $v=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}u+\beta\xi$, and the acceptance function specified there.

[F1] The algorithm supplies Borel $D$ and $\Phi_D$, extends $\Phi_D$ by $+\infty$ off $D$, proposes $\rho u+\beta\xi$ with independent $\xi\sim\mu_0$, and sets acceptance to zero when either potential value is infinite. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]]

[F2] A probability kernel has probability-measure rows and measurable event evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F3] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a probability kernel gives a measurable function of the source point. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F4] For a measure $\lambda$ and nonnegative measurable function $f$, the set function $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\lambda$ is a measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]

[F5] The preimage of a Borel set under a continuous map is Borel. [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]

[F6] Since $H$ is separable by the algorithm, let $D$ be a countable dense subset. The norm topology is the induced metric topology, whose positive-radius balls are open; the norm balls with centers in $D$ and positive rational radii are countable and form a base: if $x\in U$ with $U$ open, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then choose $d\in D$ with $\|d-x\|<r/3$ and a rational $s$ with $\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$; the triangle inequality gives $x\in B(d,s)\subseteq U$. Thus $H$ is second-countable. The Borel sigma- algebra on $H\times H$ therefore equals $\mathcal B(H)\otimes\mathcal B(H)$. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]] [[def-separable-space]] [[def-second-countable-space]] [[thm-product-of-countable]] [[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]] [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] [[def-metric-ball]] [[def-metric-topology]] [[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]] [[lem-subset-of-countable]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F7] Composing a measurable function with a Borel scalar function preserves measurability; the real exponential is continuous by the supplied smoothness result, and finite arithmetic and lattice operations preserve measurability. [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and algorithm inputs in the Statement.

1.1 For each Borel set $B$ in the extended potential range, the preimage $\bar\Phi^{-1}(B)$ is the union of $D\cap\Phi_D^{-1}(B)$ and $H\setminus D$ when $+\infty\in B$, and is just $D\cap\Phi_D^{-1}(B)$ otherwise. Since $D$ is Borel and $\Phi_D$ is Borel on the trace Borel structure of $D$, every such preimage is Borel in $H$. Thus the extended potential used by the algorithm is Borel. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and define $Q_\beta(u,B)=\int_H\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)$ for Borel $B\subseteq H$. For fixed $u$, this is the pushforward of the probability $\mu_0$ under the continuous map $z\mapsto\rho u+\beta z$, so it is a probability measure in $B$. The joint map $(u,z)\mapsto\rho u+\beta z$ is continuous; by [F6], its Borel preimages are product-measurable for $\mathcal B(H)\otimes\mathcal B(H)$. Hence $(u,z)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)$ is product-measurable. The constant kernel $u\mapsto\mu_0$ is a probability kernel, so [F3] makes $u\mapsto Q_\beta(u,B)$ measurable. Therefore $Q_\beta$ is a probability kernel by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, given, construct]

2.1 The finite-potential set $E=\{u:\bar\Phi(u)<+\infty\}$ is Borel by step 1.1. The coordinate projections on $H\times H$ are continuous and hence Borel by [F5]; [F6] identifies their source Borel sigma-algebra with the product sigma-algebra. Composing them with the Borel $\bar\Phi$ makes $(u,v)\mapsto\bar\Phi(u)$ and $(u,v)\mapsto\bar\Phi(v)$ Borel. On $E\times E$ their difference is real- valued and Borel, and [F7] makes its exponential Borel. Extending $\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}$ by $0$ off $E\times E$ therefore makes the algorithm's $\alpha$ a Borel function with values in $[0,1]$. Put $a(u)=\int_H\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)$. By [F3], $a$ is measurable; the probability rows of $Q_\beta$ give $0\le a(u)\le1$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

3.1 For each $u$ and Borel $A\subseteq H$, define $$P_\beta(u,A)=\int_A\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)+\mathbf1_A(u)(1-a(u)).$$ The first term is a measure in $A$ by [F4] and step 2.1. The second term is also a measure: among any pairwise-disjoint sequence of sets, at most one contains $u$, so the indicator of their union is the sum of their indicators at $u$. Their sum has total mass $a(u)+1-a(u)=1$. For fixed $A$, the first term is measurable in $u$ by [F3], and the second is measurable because both $\mathbf1_A(u)$ and $a(u)$ are measurable. Thus $P_\beta$ is a probability kernel by [F2]. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, and 3.1 establish that the potential extension, the proposal, the acceptance function, and the accept-reject transition have the claimed Borel and probability properties. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Example

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $D(F)\subseteq X$, $F:D(F)\to Y$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. Fix $x^\dagger\in D(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}R$, $y=F(x^\dagger)$, $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, $1\le p<\infty$, $A>0$, $0<\mu<1$, $0\le\beta<1$, and $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Write $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$, and suppose

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+A\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^{p\mu}\qquad(x\in D(F),\ R(x)\le R_0).$$

For data $y^\delta$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, suppose $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$ and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ satisfies $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$, where $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Set $c_p=2^{1-p}/p$, $H(q):=\sup_{s\ge0}(As^\mu-qs)$, and choose $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta^{p(1-\mu)}$. Then $H(c_p/\alpha)\asymp\delta^{p\mu}$ and $\alpha H(c_p/\alpha)\asymp\delta^p$. The fixed-scale conjugate and penalty-index conditions hold. Hence $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\delta^{p\mu})$ and $\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$; if $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\delta^{p\mu/s})$.

[[lem-ip-index-function-young-conjugate-bound|Conjugate error bound]]

[[thm-ip-vsc-nonlinear-regularization-rate|Banach VSC rate theorem]]

[Frederic Weidling, *Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs*, equation (2.25a)](https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/bitstream/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-411-6/weidling.pdf?sequence=1)

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography*, equation (1.32a)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The conditions in the Example hold, with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta^{p(1-\mu)}$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-vsc-nonlinear-regularization-rate]]: under the VSC, approximate-minimizer tolerance, and conjugate parameter coupling, the Bregman distance is $O(H(c_p/\alpha))$ and the residual is $O(\delta)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-index-function-young-conjugate-bound]]: $H(q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ is the conjugate term in the residual/Bregman bound.

[A1] $A>0$, $0<\mu<1$, and $p\ge1$ are fixed, independent of $\delta$.

## Verification


1.1 For $q>0$, the function $s\mapsto As^\mu-qs$ has derivative $A\mu s^{\mu-1}-q$, which decreases from $+\infty$ to $-q$ and vanishes only at $s_q=(A\mu/q)^{1/(1-\mu)}$. The function is increasing before $s_q$ and decreasing after it, with value $0$ at $s=0$ and limit $-\infty$ as $s\to\infty$, so this point is its global maximizer. Under the additional lower bound with $c_R,s>0$, division by $c_R$ gives $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\delta^{p\mu})$; taking the positive $s$-th root gives the norm rate. ## Statement

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $h\in\mathbb R^n$ use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|h_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$. Let $S$ consist of the first $s$ indices, and partition $S^c$ in this same order into consecutive nonempty blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$ of size $s$, with only the last block possibly smaller; if $S^c=\varnothing$, take $q=0$. Then
$$\|h_{S^c}\|_2\le \|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|One-based finite coordinate restrictions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one- and two-norms]]

[[def-canonical-natural|Canonical real image of the natural scalar $s$]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Triangle inequality for the finite-dimensional two-norm]]

[[lem-of-naturals-positive|Positivity and strict increase of canonical natural scalars]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3, proof of Theorem 4.25, printed pp. 89–90](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1, Theorem 2.2, printed p. 6](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a vector $h\in\mathbb R^n$, the deterministic ordered coordinate list $j_1,\ldots,j_n$, its first-$s$ set $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, and the finite successive tail blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: $h_S$ agrees with $h$ on $S$ and is zero on $S^c$; the coordinate labels are one-based with label $j$ identified with library coordinate $j-1$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|v\|_1=\sum_j|v_j|$ and $\|v\|_2=(\sum_j|v_j|^2)^{1/2}$ on finite-dimensional real coordinate spaces.

[F3] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm and obeys the triangle inequality.

[F4] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and a sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative.

[F5] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: for nonnegative $a,b$, $a^2\le b^2$ implies $a\le b$.

[F6] [[def-canonical-natural]]: a natural number used as a real scalar denotes its canonical real image.

[F7] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: the canonical real image of $s$ is positive for $s\ge1$; if $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers, then their canonical real images satisfy $k_r\le s$.

## Proof
1.1 If $q=0$, then $S^c=\varnothing$ and the conclusion is $0\le\|h_S\|_2$. If $q\ge1$, write $r=|T_1|\le s$. The order gives $T_1=\{j_{s+1},\ldots,j_{s+r}\}$ and $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, with $|h_{j_{s+k}}|\le|h_{j_k}|$ for every $1\le k\le r$. Termwise squaring and finite-sum monotonicity therefore give $\|h_{T_1}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_{s+k}}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_k}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^s|h_{j_k}|^2=\|h_S\|_2^2.$ Both norms are nonnegative, so [F5] gives $\|h_{T_1}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For each $2\le r\le q$, the preceding block $T_{r-1}$ has size $s$. Its last ordered coordinate has magnitude no greater than any earlier entry, hence no greater than the average magnitude on $T_{r-1}$. Every entry of $T_r$ is no greater than that last entry. Put $c=\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1/s$. Then each entry of $T_r$ has magnitude at most $c$. If $k_r=|T_r|$, termwise comparison gives $$\|h_{T_r}\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in T_r}|h_j|^2\le k_r c^2\le s c^2=\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1^2}{s},$$ using $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers: padding the sum of $k_r$ copies of the nonnegative number $c^2$ by the remaining nonnegative copies gives the sum of $s$ copies, by [F4]; [F6,F7] interpret these counts as real scalars. Since both sides are nonnegative, [F5] gives $\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ The blocks are disjoint and finite. By [F6], [F7], the triangle inequality, step 1.1, and this block bound, $\|h_{S^c}\|_2=\Big\|\sum_{r=1}^q h_{T_r}\Big\|_2\le\sum_{r=1}^q\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac1{\sqrt{s}}\sum_{r=1}^{q-1}\|h_{T_r}\|_1\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ This proves the claimed estimate, including a final block smaller than $s$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The tie-breaking rule makes the block partition deterministic. The proof uses only finite coordinate comparisons and the Euclidean triangle inequality; no choice axiom is used.

## Statement

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Use one-based coordinate labels
$j=1,\ldots,n$, with coordinate $j$ identified with the library's coordinate
$j-1$. Assume that
$$\sum_{j\in S}|h_j|<\sum_{j\notin S}|h_j|$$
for every nonzero $h\in\mathbb R^n$ with $Ah=0$ and every
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|S|\le s$. Then there is a constant
$\rho\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\sum_{j\in S}|h_j|\le\rho\sum_{j\notin S}|h_j|$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ with $Ah=0$ and every
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|S|\le s$. The estimate is only on the exact
kernel and gives no bound for vectors with $Ah\ne0$.

## Statement references

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one-norm and Euclidean norm]]

[[def-euclidean-inner-product|The Euclidean inner product and norm]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Norm properties of finite-dimensional p-norms]]

[[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric|Continuity of finite-dimensional norms]]

[[lem-finite-set-has-max|A finite set of real numbers has a maximum]]

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm|Cauchy–Schwarz for the Euclidean inner product]]

[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values|Heine–Borel and extreme-value theorem in finite dimensions]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.2, Definition 4.11 and Remark 4.16, pp. 82–85](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ satisfying the strict nullspace inequalities in the Statement, and $\ker A:=\{h\in\mathbb R^n:Ah=0\}$.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: for every nonzero $h\in\ker A$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, $\|h_S\|_1<\|h_{S^c}\|_1$, where $h_S$ is zero outside $S$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|$ on $\mathbb R^n$.

[F3] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}$ on $\mathbb R^n$.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for $a,u,v\in\mathbb R^n$, $|\langle a,u-v\rangle|\le\|a\|_2\|u-v\|_2$.

[F5] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: both $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ are norms on $\mathbb R^n$, and $d_2(u,v)=\|u-v\|_2$ for $n\ge1$.

[F6] [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]: a norm satisfies absolute homogeneity, $N(\lambda v)=|\lambda|N(v)$.

[F7] [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]: every norm on $\mathbb R^n$ is continuous for the Euclidean metric.

[F8] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ are compact, and continuous real-valued functions on nonempty compact subsets attain their maxima; this result is choice-free.

[F9] [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]: every nonempty finite set of real numbers has a maximum.

[F10] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums are monotone termwise; every nonnegative term is at most its sum, and adjoining nonnegative terms cannot decrease the sum.

[F11] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: under its coordinate relabeling, $(Au)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}u_j$ for each row $i$.

[F12] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: for the row vector $r_i$ with coordinates $(r_i)_j=A_{ij}$, $\langle r_i,u\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}u_j$.

[F13] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: additivity and scalar multiplication of finite sums give $\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(u_j-v_j)=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}u_j-\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}v_j$.

[F14] [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]: for every norm $N$, $|N(u)-N(v)|\le N(u-v)$.

[F15] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: for nonnegative reals $a,b$, $a\le b$ if and only if $a^2\le b^2$.

## Proof

1.1 If $\ker A=\{0\}$, choose $\rho=1/2$. The only $h\in\ker A$ is zero, so both sides of the required inequality are zero for every $S$. Now suppose $\ker A\ne\{0\}$ and define $K:=\{h\in\ker A:\|h\|_2=1\}$. This set is nonempty by normalizing a nonzero kernel vector, since [F5] makes its norm positive. To show $K$ is closed, fix $x\notin K$. If $Ax\ne0$, choose a row $i$ with $c:=(Ax)_i\ne0$ and let $r_i$ be that row as a vector in $\mathbb R^n$. By [F14], $|\|y\|_2-\|x\|_2|\le\|y-x\|_2$, so $\|y-x\|_2<\delta$ precludes $\|y\|_2=1$ and again $y\notin K$. Hence every point outside $K$ has a ball disjoint from $K$, so $K$ is closed. [given, F3, F4, F5, F8, F11, F12, F13, F14, construct, choose]

2.1 Fix $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$ and define $P_S,P_{S^c}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ by $P_Su:=u_S$ and $P_{S^c}u:=u_{S^c}$. For all $u,v\in\mathbb R^n$ and every coordinate $j$, $|(P_Su-P_Sv)_j|\le|u_j-v_j|$; both sides are nonnegative, so the forward implication in [F15] and then [F10] give $\|P_Su-P_Sv\|_2^2\le\|u-v\|_2^2$. Both Euclidean norms are nonnegative by [F5], so the converse implication in [F15] yields $\|P_Su-P_Sv\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2$. The same argument applies to $P_{S^c}$, making both coordinate projections $1$-Lipschitz, hence continuous for $d_2$. Since $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm by [F5] and every norm on $\mathbb R^n$ is continuous for $d_2$ by [F7], the compositions $a_S(h):=\|h_S\|_1$ and $b_S(h):=\|h_{S^c}\|_1$ are continuous. By [F8] it attains a maximum $q_S$ on $K$, and [F1] at a maximizing point gives $0\le q_S<1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, F8, F10, F15, algebra]

3.1 There are finitely many sets $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, and this family is nonempty because it contains $\varnothing$. Therefore [F9] gives $q:=\max_{|S|\le s}q_S<1$. Choose any $h\in K$ and a coordinate $j$ with $h_j\ne0$; then $S=\{j\}$ is admissible because $s\ge1$, and [F2] gives $r_S(h)>0$, so $q>0$. Set $\rho:=(1+q)/2$; then $q<\rho<1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, F1, F2, F9, choose, algebra]

4.1 Let $h\in\ker A$. If $h=0$, the required inequality is immediate. Otherwise $\widetilde h:=h/\|h\|_2$ belongs to $K$. For every admissible $S$, [F6] gives $r_S(h)=r_S(\widetilde h)\le q<\rho$, so $\|h_S\|_1\le\rho\|h_{S^c}\|_1$. This proves the estimate with one constant for all $S$ and all kernel vectors. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ satisfy the strict nullspace property of order
$s$. Use one-based coordinate labels $j=1,\ldots,n$, with coordinate $j$
identified with the library's coordinate $j-1$. If $x^\dagger\in\mathbb R^n$
has at most $s$ nonzero coordinates, then
$x^\dagger$ is the unique minimizer of
$$\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|$$
over all $z\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfying $Az=Ax^\dagger$. This is a noiseless
exact-data result; it makes no exact-recovery or support-recovery assertion for
noisy observations.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|Strict nullspace property and coordinate conventions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one-norm]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Triangle inequality for the finite-dimensional one-norm]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.1, Theorems 4.4–4.5, pp. 79–80](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Bandeira, *Ten Lectures and Forty-Two Open Problems in the Mathematics of Data Science*, §6.3, pp. 106–107](https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-s096-topics-in-mathematics-of-data-science-fall-2015/5f0f7205d1cf274e80d77345a7edbf2a_MIT18_S096F15_TenLec.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge1$, an integer $1\le s\le n$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ satisfying the strict nullspace property of order $s$, and a vector $x^\dagger\in\mathbb R^n$ with at most $s$ nonzero coordinates.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: for every nonzero $h\in\ker A$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, $\|h_S\|_1<\|h_{S^c}\|_1$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|u\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^n|u_j|$ for $u\in\mathbb R^n$.

[F3] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: the p=1 formula is a norm on $\mathbb R^n$.

[F4] [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]: every norm $N$ satisfies the triangle inequality $N(u+v)\le N(u)+N(v)$.

[F5] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: under its coordinate relabeling, $(Au)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}u_j$ for each row $i$.

[F6] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums are additive, so $\sum_{j=1}^n(b_j-c_j)=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j-\sum_{j=1}^n c_j$ for real lists.

## Proof

1.1 Let $S:=\{j\in[n]:x_j^\dagger\ne0\}$, so $|S|\le s$. For any feasible $z\ne x^\dagger$, put $h:=z-x^\dagger$. For each row $i$, [F5] and [F6] give $(Ah)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(z_j-x_j^\dagger)=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}z_j-\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j^\dagger=(Az)_i-(Ax^\dagger)_i=0$, so $h\in\ker A$ and $h\ne0$. Hence [F1] gives $\|h_S\|_1<\|h_{S^c}\|_1$. [given, F1, F5, F6, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm, so [F4] gives its triangle inequality. On $S$, $z_S=x^\dagger_S+h_S$, hence $\|x^\dagger\|_1=\|x^\dagger_S\|_1=\|z_S-h_S\|_1\le\|z_S\|_1+\|h_S\|_1$. On $S^c$, $x^\dagger$ vanishes and $z_{S^c}=h_{S^c}$, so $z=z_S+h_{S^c}$ with disjoint coordinate supports and $\|z\|_1=\|z_S\|_1+\|h_{S^c}\|_1$. By step 1.1, this is strictly greater than $\|z_S\|_1+\|h_S\|_1\ge\|x^\dagger\|_1$. Thus every feasible vector distinct from $x^\dagger$ has strictly larger objective, and $x^\dagger$, which is feasible, is the unique minimizer. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$
be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable everywhere with
$x\mapsto F'(x)$ continuous in operator norm. For $s>0$, write
$$B_s(x_0):=\{x\in X:\|x-x_0\|_X<s\}.$$
Suppose $B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$ for some $r>0$, $x^\dagger\in B_r(x_0)$,
and $F(x^\dagger)=y$. Assume there are constants $M,c>0$ such that, for every
$x,\tilde x\in B_{2r}(x_0)$,
$$\|F'(x)\|\le M,$$
$$\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)-F'(x)(x-\tilde x)\|_Y\le c\|x-\tilde x\|_X\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)\|_Y.$$
Fix $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and $\tau>1/\sigma$. Put
$$e_0:=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X$$
and assume
$$e_0<\min\left\{r,\frac{\sigma\tau-1}{c(1+\tau)},\frac{1-\sigma}{2c}\right\}.$$
Set
$$\gamma:=\frac{\sigma\tau}{1+ce_0(1+\tau)};$$
the hypotheses give $\gamma>1$. For each exact iteration, use this $\gamma$ in
the range-approximation margin of the regularized LM procedure and select any
positive parameter satisfying its residual-forcing equality.
For every $\delta>0$ and $y^\delta\in Y$ satisfying
$\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, start at $x_0^\delta=x_0$ and, at each state
before stopping, let $h_n$ minimize
$$h\longmapsto\frac12\|F'(x_n^\delta)h+F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha_n}{2}\|h\|_X^2$$
for a selected $\alpha_n>0$ satisfying
$$\|F'(x_n^\delta)h_n+F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=\sigma\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y,$$
and set $x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+h_n$. Let $N_\delta$ be the first
$n\in\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ such that
$$\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y\le\tau\delta.$$
Then this exact iteration is well-defined up to a finite first discrepancy
index $N_\delta$. Set
$$q:=\frac{\sigma+ce_0}{1-ce_0},\qquad K:=1+\|F(x_0)-y\|_Y,\qquad \delta_0:=\min\left\{1,\frac K\tau\right\}.$$
Here $q\in(0,1)$ and $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm. For
$0<\delta\le\delta_0$,
$$N_\delta\le1+\frac{\log(K/(\tau\delta))}{-\log q}.$$
Consequently $N_\delta=O(1+|\log\delta|)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, with
constants depending only on the fixed problem and displayed parameters. A
finite run with update budget at least $N_\delta$ and successful exact calls
returns this first crossing; a shorter budget may return
`budget-exhausted`. No convergence rate for $x_{N_\delta}^\delta$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; real Hilbert spaces $X,Y$; an open domain $U$; a continuously Fréchet differentiable map $F:U\to Y$; $B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$; an exact solution $x^\dagger\in B_r(x_0)$ with $F(x^\dagger)=y$; constants $M,c>0$; $\sigma\in(0,1)$; $\tau>1/\sigma$; the stated smallness bound on $e_0$; and positive noise $\delta$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|\le\delta$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the sole choice axiom assumed for Hilbert adjoints and the shifted normal equations ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] On the local ball, the product remainder is bounded by $c\|x-\tilde x\|\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)\|$ ([[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition]]).

[F2] If $\|x-x^\dagger\|\le e_0$ and $\|F(x)-y^\delta\|>\tau\delta$, then the linearized residual at $x^\dagger$ is at most $[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]/\tau$ times the current residual; when $\gamma=\sigma\tau/[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]>1$, this is at most $\sigma/\gamma$ times the current residual ([[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation]]).

[F3] The algorithm checks discrepancy before updates, uses the exact regularized linearized minimizer and the residual-forcing equality, and returns the first crossing when exact calls and its finite cap permit ([[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F4] Under the range-approximation condition, the exact step obeys
$$\|e_n\|^2-\|e_n+h_n\|^2\ge\|h_n\|^2+\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma^2}{\gamma\alpha_n}\|F(x_n)-y^\delta\|^2,$$
and if $\|F'(x_n)\|\le M$, then $\alpha_n\le\sigma M^2/(1-\sigma)$ ([[lem-ip-lm-fejer-decrease-and-parameter-bound]]).

[F5] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing, satisfies the quotient law, and is negative on $(0,1)$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

[F6] For every real bound $b$, some natural number exceeds $b$ ([[lem-cauchy-reals-archimedean]]).

[F7] The real Hilbert norm satisfies the triangle inequality ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

[F8] A Fréchet derivative is a bounded linear map, and its norm is the operator norm defined on bounded linear maps ([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]], [[def-operator-norm]]).

[F9] For a nonzero residual and a vector meeting the range-approximation margin, the regularized linearized least-squares problem has a unique minimizer and some positive parameter attains the residual-forcing equality ([[lem-ip-lm-step-existence-and-residual-forcing]]).

## Proof


1.1 Define $\gamma:=\sigma\tau/[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]$. The bound $e_0<(\sigma\tau-1)/(c(1+\tau))$ gives $1+ce_0(1+\tau)<\sigma\tau$, so $\gamma>1$. Since $e_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X\ge0$ and $c>0$, the other smallness bound gives $0\le ce_0<(1-\sigma)/2$. Hence $1-ce_0>0$; also $\sigma+ce_0>0$ because $\sigma>0$, and $2ce_0<1-\sigma$ gives $\sigma+ce_0<1-ce_0$. Thus $q=(\sigma+ce_0)/(1-ce_0)$ lies in $(0,1)$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For each pre-stop index, the given derivative bound and [F8] give $\|F'(x_n^\delta)\|\le M$. Thus [F4] and $\alpha_n\le\sigma M^2/(1-\sigma)$ give $e_n^2-e_{n+1}^2\ge D\,R_n^2,\qquad D:=\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma(1-\sigma)}{\gamma M^2}>0,$ where $R_n:=\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y$. [F4, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 We construct the exact path up to its first crossing by finite induction. Initially $x_0^\delta=x_0\in B_{2r}(x_0)$ and $e_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|$. Suppose $x_n^\delta\in B_{2r}(x_0)$ and $e_n:=\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|\le e_0$. If its residual is at most $\tau\delta$, the path stops. Otherwise [F2] with $e=e_0$ gives the range-approximation hypothesis with the $\gamma$ of step 1.1. Since $R_n>\tau\delta>0$, [F9] supplies the positive forcing parameter and unique minimizer. Applying [F4] shows $e_{n+1}\le e_n$ and $\|h_n\|\le e_n$. Hence $e_{n+1}\le e_0$ and $\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x_0\|_X\le\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X+e_0\le2e_0<2r,$ so the next state remains in the local ball and the induction continues. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F7, F9, given, induction]

3.1 For $m\ge1$, if no crossing has occurred in the first $m$ updates, then $R_n>\tau\delta$ for $0\le n<m$. Summing step 1.2 telescopes and yields $D m\tau^2\delta^2< D\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}R_n^2\le e_0^2.$ By [F6], choose a natural $m>e_0^2/(D\tau^2\delta^2)$. The displayed inequality is impossible for that $m$, so a crossing occurs at a finite index $N_\delta$. Summing step 1.2 through $N_\delta-1$ also gives $N_\delta\le e_0^2/(D\tau^2\delta^2)$. [F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, given, choose, algebra]

3.2 Fix $n<N_\delta$ and set $T_n:=F'(x_n^\delta)$, $h_n:=x_{n+1}^\delta-x_n^\delta$, $q_n:=y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)-T_nh_n$, and $\Delta_n:=F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-F(x_n^\delta)-T_nh_n.$ Both iterates lie in $B_{2r}(x_0)$ by step 2.1. Applying [F1] to the ordered pair $(x_n^\delta,x_{n+1}^\delta)$ gives $\|\Delta_n\|_Y\le c\|h_n\|_X\|F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y$. The forcing rule gives $\|q_n\|_Y=\sigma R_n$, while $F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-y^\delta=-q_n+\Delta_n.$ Therefore, with $R_{n+1}:=\|F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y$, $R_{n+1}\le\sigma R_n+c\|h_n\|_X(R_{n+1}+R_n).$ Using $\|h_n\|\le e_n\le e_0$ from [F4] and $1-ce_0>0$ from step 1.1 yields $R_{n+1}\le\frac{\sigma+ce_0}{1-ce_0}R_n=qR_n.$ [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $K:=1+\|F(x_0)-y\|_Y$ and $\delta_0:=\min\{1,K/\tau\}$. By [F7] and the data-noise bound, $R_0\le K$ for $0<\delta\le\delta_0$. If $N_\delta\ge2$, the first-crossing definition gives $\tau\delta<R_{N_\delta-1}$, while repeated application of step 3.2 gives $R_{N_\delta-1}\le q^{N_\delta-1}R_0\le q^{N_\delta-1}K$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, $\log(\tau\delta/K)<(N_\delta-1)\log q$; by [F5], $\log q<0$, so division reverses the inequality and gives $N_\delta\le1+\frac{\log(K/(\tau\delta))}{-\log q}.$ The same bound holds for $N_\delta=0$ or $1$, since $\delta\le K/\tau$ makes its right side at least $1$. Finally, for $\delta\le\delta_0\le1$, [F5] gives $\log\frac{K}{\tau\delta}\le\left|\log\frac K\tau\right|+|\log\delta|,$ so, with $C:=1+[1+|\log(K/\tau)|]/(-\log q)$, the displayed bound is at most $C(1+|\log\delta|)$, with $C$ independent of $y^\delta$ and $\delta$. By [F3], a finite run with cap at least $N_\delta$ and successful exact calls returns this crossing. The proof asserts no convergence rate for the stopped iterate. [F3, F5, F7, step 3.2, given, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The source's logarithmic count uses the product-type remainder condition and a sufficiently small start. Positive noise is essential for finite discrepancy stopping; the B-page zero-noise counterexample verifies this boundary. This theorem proves an index bound only, not convergence of the stopped solution or an error rate.

## Definition

Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

## Statement

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

## Remarks

An ESS is functional-specific and is not a substitute for a Monte Carlo standard
error. The variance bound in this Proposition is a population statement under
its chain assumptions; it does not validate a finite-chain empirical ESS
estimate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, the complete error budget when its pathwise bound is used, and a stationary Markov chain in the separate sample-error branch.

[F1] Total variation is the event supremum $\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$; it has no half-factor. [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F2] If $\mu,\nu$ are probability measures and $|f|\le M$, then $|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}$. [[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations]]

[F3] The error budget consists of the six absolute adjacent differences from $\mu_\star(f)$ through $\bar f_{b,N}$, and its Monte Carlo component is pathwise. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F4] A stationary chain has marginal law $\pi_K$ at every time, and the covariance of $f(X_i),f(X_j)$ depends only on the lag $|j-i|$. [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]] [[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]

[F5] For square-integrable real random variables, variance is the expected squared centered value and covariance is the expected product of centered values. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

## Statement

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian surface with smooth boundary. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ for its outward unit normal and use the curvature convention $R(A,B)C=\nabla_A\nabla_BC-\nabla_B\nabla_AC-\nabla_{[A,B]}C$. Write $D_tJ=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}J$; a Jacobi field along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth field $J$ satisfying $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$. Assume $g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0$ for every nonzero boundary-tangent vector $w$, no nonzero Jacobi field on any positive-length unit-speed geodesic segment vanishes at both endpoints, and every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. Set $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$ and $\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,-\nu_{\mathrm{out}})>0\}$. For a real-valued $f\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ,\mathbb R)$ and $(x,v)\in\partial_+SM$, let $\gamma_{x,v}$ be the unit-speed geodesic with initial data $(x,v)$, let $\tau_+(x,v)$ be its first positive boundary-exit time, and define
$$
I_0f(x,v)=\int_0^{\tau_+(x,v)} f(\gamma_{x,v}(t))\,dt.
$$
Then $I_0f=0$ on $\partial_+SM$ implies $f=0$ on $M$. No orientability assumption on $M$ is required.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Definition of simple surfaces and incoming geodesic data]]

[[lem-ip-surface-geodesic-flow-index-form-and-transport|Transport, Santaló, and index-form facts for simple surfaces]]

[[lem-ip-pestov-identity-for-geodesic-data|Pestov identity for geodesic data]]

[[lem-ip-orientation-cover-preserves-simplicity|Orientation-cover lifting of simple geometry and X-ray data]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A simple compact connected nonempty smooth Riemannian surface $M$, a real scalar $f\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$, and zero boundary geodesic X-ray data $I_0f=0$.

[F1] [[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform]]: simple means strictly convex boundary, no conjugate points, and finite forward/backward exit times; $I_0f$ is the integral of $f$ over each unit-speed boundary-to-boundary geodesic.

[F2] [[lem-ip-orientation-cover-preserves-simplicity]]: every connected component of the tangent orientation cover with pullback metric is compact, connected, oriented, and simple; its projection is a local isometry onto $M$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-orientation-cover-preserves-simplicity]]: $I_{0,C}(f\circ\pi)(\widetilde z)=I_{0,M}f(\pi(\widetilde z))$ for every incoming state $\widetilde z$ on a component $C$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-surface-geodesic-flow-index-form-and-transport]]: zero scalar data gives a smooth compactly supported transport primitive $u$ with $Xu=-f$ and $u|_{\partial SM}=0$; $V$ is tangent to $\partial SM$.

[F5] [[lem-ip-pestov-identity-for-geodesic-data]]: for smooth real $u$ vanishing on the boundary of an oriented simple surface, $\|VXu\|^2=\|XVu\|^2-(KVu,Vu)+\|Xu\|^2$.

[F6] [[lem-ip-surface-geodesic-flow-index-form-and-transport]]: $d\Sigma=dV_g(x)\,dS_x(v)$ and Santaló's formula is $\int_{SM}h\,d\Sigma=\int_{\partial_+SM}\mu\int_0^{\tau_+}h(\varphi_t(z))\,dt\,d\Sigma_\partial$ for continuous $h$; [[def-riemannian-volume-density]]: in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$.

[F7] [[lem-ip-surface-geodesic-flow-index-form-and-transport]]: $\mathcal I_\gamma(Y,Y)=\int_0^L(|D_tY|^2-g(R(Y,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma,Y))\,dt$ for endpoint-zero normal fields.

[F8] [[lem-ip-surface-geodesic-flow-index-form-and-transport]]: the index form is positive for each nonzero endpoint-zero normal field.

[F9] [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-riemannian-geometry]]: the metric has a unique Levi-Civita connection.

[F10] [[def-levi-civita-connection]]: the Levi-Civita connection is metric-compatible and torsion-free.

[F11] [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]]: $R(A,B)C=\nabla_A\nabla_BC-\nabla_B\nabla_AC-\nabla_{[A,B]}C$.

[F12] [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]: $\operatorname{Rm}(A,B,C,D)=g(R(A,B)C,D)$.

## Proof

1.1 If $f=0$, the conclusion holds; assume $f\ne0$ for contradiction. Let $C$ be any connected component of the tangent orientation cover of $M$ and let $\widetilde f=f\circ\pi$ on $C$. By [F2], $C$ is a compact oriented simple surface and $I_{0,C}\widetilde f=0$. The transport conclusion of [F4] supplies $u\in C_c^\infty(SC^\circ)$ with $Xu=-\widetilde f$ and $u=0$ on $\partial SC$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 The vector field $V$ is vertical, so it differentiates functions along a fixed fibre and $V\widetilde f=0$. Applying [F4] and [F5] to $u$ gives $0=\|VXu\|^2=\|XVu\|^2-(KVu,Vu)+\|Xu\|^2$. [F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F4], $Vu=0$ on $\partial SC$: $V$ is tangent to that boundary and $u$ vanishes there. Fix any incoming unit geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to C$, and let $Q$ denote positive rotation by $90$ degrees on each oriented tangent plane. In a positive orthonormal frame $e_1,e_2=Qe_1$, metric compatibility gives $\nabla_Ae_1=\omega(A)e_2$ and $\nabla_Ae_2=-\omega(A)e_1$ for a scalar one-form $\omega$. Using $(\nabla_AQ)e_i=\nabla_A(Qe_i)-Q\nabla_Ae_i$, we get $(\nabla_AQ)e_1=-\omega(A)e_1+\omega(A)e_1=0$ and $(\nabla_AQ)e_2=-\omega(A)e_2+\omega(A)e_2=0$, so $\nabla Q=0$ and $n(t)=Q\dot\gamma(t)$ is a parallel unit normal. The scalar function $w(t)=Vu(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))$ has $w(0)=w(L)=0$, and put $Y(t)=w(t)n(t)$; then $|D_tY|^2=(w')^2$. The positive frame $(\dot\gamma,n)$ gives $K=g(R(\dot\gamma,n)n,\dot\gamma)$. The curvature definition gives $R(n,\dot\gamma)=-R(\dot\gamma,n)$; metric compatibility and the scalar commutator identity give $0=A(Bg(C,D))-B(Ag(C,D))-[A,B]g(C,D)=g(R(A,B)C,D)+g(C,R(A,B)D)$. Taking $A=\dot\gamma$, $B=n$, $C=\dot\gamma$, and $D=n$ yields $g(R(\dot\gamma,n)\dot\gamma,n)=-K$, hence $g(R(n,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma,n)=K$. Therefore $\int_0^L((XVu)^2-K(Vu)^2)(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))\,dt=\mathcal I_\gamma(Y,Y)\ge0$, with equality allowed only when $Y=0$, by [F8]. [F4, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Apply Santaló's formula from [F6] to the continuous function $(XVu)^2-K(Vu)^2$ on $SC$. Step 3.1 shows that its integral over each boundary-to-boundary geodesic is nonnegative; the incoming flux weight is positive. Hence $\|XVu\|^2-(KVu,Vu)=\int_{SC}((XVu)^2-K(Vu)^2)\,d\Sigma\ge0$. [F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $Xu=-\widetilde f$, the remaining term in step 2.1 is $\|Xu\|^2=\|\widetilde f\|^2$. Under the standing assumption $f\ne0$, choose an interior point $x$ with $f(x)\ne0$; continuity gives an open neighborhood on which $f$ is nonzero. By [F2], $\pi|_C$ is onto and a local diffeomorphism, so $\widetilde f$ is nonzero on a nonempty open subset of $C$; [F6] supplies a smooth positive Liouville density, making $\|\widetilde f\|^2>0$. This contradicts step 2.1 together with the nonnegative quantity in step 4.1. Therefore $f=0$. [F2, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, choose] ∎

## Definition

Let $M$ be a smooth two-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $\det T_xM=\Lambda^2T_xM$ be the determinant line of its tangent space. An orientation of $T_xM$ is a positive ray $o_x$ in this line. The **tangent orientation double cover** is the set
$$
\widetilde M=\{(x,o_x):x\in M,\ o_x\text{ is an orientation of }T_xM\},\qquad \pi(x,o_x)=x.
$$
For a boundary chart $\phi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb H^2$, let $o_\phi(x)$ be the ray obtained by applying $\det(d\phi_x^{-1})$ to the standard positive ray in $\det\mathbb R^2$. Give $\widetilde M$ the smooth boundary-chart structure whose two local sheets over $U$ are $\{(x,o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$ and $\{(x,-o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$, each with coordinate map $(x,\pm o_\phi(x))\mapsto\phi(x)$. On an overlap with a second chart $\psi$, the sheet sign changes by $\operatorname{sgn}\det D(\psi\circ\phi^{-1})$; this sign is locally constant, so the sheet transitions are smooth half-space transitions. Thus $\pi$ is the associated two-sheeted smooth covering map, including over the boundary. The involution $\tau(x,o_x)=(x,-o_x)$ exchanges the sheets. The canonical orientation of $\widetilde M$ at $(x,o_x)$ is the ray $(\det d\pi_{(x,o_x)})^{-1}(o_x)$ in $\det T_{(x,o_x)}\widetilde M$.

## Statement

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian surface with smooth boundary, and assume its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping. Let $\pi:\widetilde M\to M$ be the tangent orientation double cover, give $\widetilde M$ the pullback metric $\widetilde g=\pi^*g$, and let $C$ be any connected component of $\widetilde M$. Then $C$ is a compact, connected, oriented simple Riemannian surface with smooth boundary, and $\pi|_C:C\to M$ is a local isometry mapping $\partial C$ onto $\partial M$. For every $f\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$, define $\widetilde f=f\circ\pi$. For each incoming unit vector $\widetilde z\in\partial_+SC$, the scalar geodesic X-ray transform satisfies
$$
I_{0,C}\widetilde f(\widetilde z)=I_{0,M}f(\pi(\widetilde z)).
$$
In particular, zero data for $f$ on $M$ gives zero data for $\widetilde f$ on every component $C$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Definition of simple surfaces and the scalar geodesic X-ray transform]]

[[def-ip-tangent-orientation-double-cover|Definition of the tangent orientation double cover]]

[[thm-compactness-is-invariant-under-finite-sheeted-coverings|Compactness theorem for finite-sheeted covers]]

[[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps|Path lifting theorem for covering maps]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact connected nonempty simple Riemannian surface $M$, its tangent orientation double cover, a component $C$, and $f\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform]]: strict convexity means $g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0$ for nonzero boundary-tangent $w$; no conjugate points means every Jacobi field vanishing at the two endpoints of a geodesic segment is zero; nontrapping means every maximal interior unit-speed geodesic exits in both time directions in finite time.

[F2] [[def-ip-tangent-orientation-double-cover]]: $\pi:\widetilde M\to M$ is a two-sheeted smooth covering and local diffeomorphism including over the boundary; its points are tangent orientation rays and its second coordinate defines a canonical orientation.

[F3] [[thm-compactness-is-invariant-under-finite-sheeted-coverings]]: a finite-sheeted covering has compact total space exactly when its base is compact.

[F4] [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]: a Riemannian metric is a smooth positive-definite symmetric covariant two-tensor; [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-riemannian-geometry]]: each supplied smooth Riemannian metric, also up to a boundary, has a unique Levi-Civita connection.

[F5] [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]]: $R(A,B)C=\nabla_A\nabla_BC-\nabla_B\nabla_AC-\nabla_{[A,B]}C$; [[def-jacobi-field]]: a Jacobi field satisfies $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$.

[F6] [[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps]]: every path in the base and every chosen initial point in its fibre have a unique continuous lift.

[F7] [[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]]: smooth local vector fields have unique local integral curves depending smoothly on initial state.

[F8] [[thm-connected-and-locally-path-connected-implies-path-connected]]: a connected locally path-connected space is path-connected; smooth boundary charts have path-connected smaller half-ball neighborhoods.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $\pi$ is a two-sheeted covering; applying [F3] to compact $M$ shows that $\widetilde M$ is compact. In each boundary chart the two sheets are copies of the same half-space chart, so $\pi^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial\widetilde M$ and $\pi^{-1}(M^\circ)=\widetilde M^\circ$. [F2, F3, given]

1.2 Every connected component $C$ of the smooth manifold $\widetilde M$ is open, since each point has a connected chart neighborhood contained in its component, and it is closed, since connected components are closed. Thus $C$ is compact. Smooth boundary charts have path-connected smaller half-ball neighborhoods, so $M$ is locally path-connected and [F8] makes connected $M$ path-connected. Fix $\widetilde x\in C$ and any $y\in M$; lift a path from $\pi(\widetilde x)$ to $y$ starting at $\widetilde x$ by [F6]. Its connected image stays in $C$, so its endpoint lies over $y$ and $\pi(C)=M$. The canonical orientation from [F2] restricts to $C$. [F2, F6, F8, given]

2.1 The pullback $\widetilde g=\pi^*g$ is smooth and positive definite because $d\pi$ is a smooth isomorphism on each sheet and $g$ is smooth positive definite by [F4]. In the sheet coordinates of [F2], $\pi$ is the identity and the metric coefficient matrices of $\widetilde g$ and $g$ coincide. The unique Levi-Civita connections therefore have identical coordinate coefficients; the geodesic equations and curvature coefficients also coincide by [F4, F5]. Boundary normals and their second fundamental forms correspond under $d\pi$, so strict convexity of $\partial M$ gives strict convexity of $\partial C$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 If $\widetilde J$ is a Jacobi field along a geodesic segment in $C$, then [F5] and the identical local connection and curvature coefficients in step 2.1 show that $d\pi(\widetilde J)$ is a Jacobi field along the projected geodesic. If $\widetilde J$ vanishes at both endpoints, its projection vanishes there; [F1] makes the projected field zero, and invertibility of $d\pi$ gives $\widetilde J=0$. Thus $C$ has no conjugate points. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 A unit-speed geodesic in $C^\circ$ projects by step 2.1 to a unit-speed geodesic in $M^\circ$. By [F1] that projected geodesic reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. Lift each finite projected segment from the specified initial point by [F6]. In every sheet the lift solves the same geodesic ODE as the original curve, so uniqueness from [F7] makes it an extension of that curve to the exit time; the endpoint lies in $\partial C$ by step 1.1. Hence $C$ is nontrapping in both directions. Together with steps 1.2–2.1, $C$ is simple. [F1, F2, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Since $f$ is supported in the interior, $\widetilde f=f\circ\pi$ is smooth and vanishes near $\partial\widetilde M$. Its support is a closed subset of compact $\widetilde M$, hence compact, and it lies in $C^\circ$ after restriction to $C$. For an incoming $\widetilde z\in\partial_+SC$, local isometry maps its inward normal component to that of $z=\pi(\widetilde z)\in\partial_+SM$. The projected unit geodesic and the lifted unit geodesic have the same parameter and first boundary-exit time by steps 1.1 and 4.1; hence $I_{0,C}\widetilde f(\widetilde z)=\int_0^{\tau_+(z)}f(\gamma_z(t))\,dt=I_{0,M}f(z)$. This proves the transform identity and the zero-data implication. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an $n$-singular oriented knot with $n\ge0$ transverse double points and chord diagram $D\in\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$. Choose disjoint crossing balls and a common height presentation so that the two branches at every singular point are monotone in height inside their ball, all $2^n$ resolutions are strict Morse, and their height functions and number $r$ of local maxima agree outside the crossing balls. Define
$$
\Delta^n I(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i\right)I(K_\epsilon).
$$
Then $\Delta^n I(K)$ has zero homogeneous components in degrees $m<n$, its degree-$n$ component is exactly $D$, and all remaining terms have degree greater than $n$. For $n=0$, the degree-zero component is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$. The conclusion is in the unframed 4T+1T chord-diagram completion and makes no rational-coefficient claim.

The drawing shows a singular crossing and the two oriented resolutions. The plus resolution is the one with positive determinant crossing sign; the drawing fixes no analytic estimate and is not used in the proof.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, an $n$-singular oriented knot, its disjoint transverse crossing balls, and the common strict Morse height of all resolutions.

[F1] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: an $n$-singular knot has $n$ disjoint transverse double points; its $n$th finite difference is the alternating sum of the $2^n$ positive and negative resolutions.

[F2] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: $Z(K)$ is the degreewise configuration integral in the unframed 4T+1T completion, and $I(K)=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}$.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: an isolated chord is zero in the unframed target, and the 4T relation identifies the local endpoint slides.

[F4] [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: the positive crossing sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ in the positively oriented projection plane, with the positive Artin half twist assigned sign $+1$.

[F5] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates]]: each fixed-degree sum converges absolutely; contributions with an endpoint in a width-$\varepsilon$ critical needle are uniformly $O(\varepsilon)$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the countable-choice axiom used by the ambient-isotopy supplier.

[F6] [[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the normalized series is invariant under ambient isotopy, and changing a strict Morse presentation of a resolution does not change its value.

[F7] **External input — the principal symbol of the configuration integral.** Chmutov–Duzhin–Mostovoy, §8.8.1, printed pp. 239–240, equation (2) and its proof, establishes for a singular Morse tangle $T_D$ with $n$ transverse double points that its alternating unnormalized integral has no degree below $n$ and degree-$n$ term $D$ in the unframed diagram quotient. The proof treats $n=0$, the local singular two-braid, localization for an arbitrary one-singular tangle, and vertical factorization for general $n$. Its hypotheses are the same unframed configuration integral and positive-minus-negative resolution convention used here. Actual reading for this repair: both pages and the entire argument, including its one-singular localization. This is an imported theorem, not a claimed uniform estimate for every individual pairing as crossing balls shrink.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Fix a degree cutoff $N$ and work in the finite-dimensional quotient through degree $N$.

1.1 Choose pairwise disjoint balls around the $n$ singular points so each resolved pair of branches is monotone in height inside its ball. The same height function is used on every resolution, so $r(K_\epsilon)=r$ for all $\epsilon$. If necessary, move the singular knot by an isotopy supported in the balls to separate the singular heights and make the crossings monotone; each corresponding resolution is carried by the same ambient isotopy, so [F6] leaves $\Delta^n I(K)$ unchanged. [given, F1, F4, A1, F6, construct]

1.2 Expand the degree-$m$ part of $\Delta^n I(K)$ as a finite sum of pairing integrals over the resolution choices. If a pairing has no chord endpoint in the $i$th crossing ball, its integrand and diagram are independent of the sign $\epsilon_i$, because the two resolved knots agree outside that ball. Summing over $\epsilon_i=+1,-1$ therefore cancels that term. Hence every nonzero contribution to the $n$-fold difference must meet each of the $n$ balls. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply the principal-symbol theorem [F7] to the common singular Morse presentation. It gives $D_nZ(K)_m=0$ for $m<n$ and $D_nZ(K)_n=D$. The local hypotheses hold by step 1.1 and the unframed target agrees by [F2, F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For one singular point, let $w_\pm(t)=z_{1,\pm}(t)-z_{2,\pm}(t)$ be the relative complex coordinate of its two monotone branches in the positive and negative resolutions. The loop obtained by following $w_+$ and then the reverse of $w_-$ winds once positively around $0$: the two resolutions are the opposite half-turns of the relative vector. Hence $\frac1{2\pi i}\left(\int d\log w_+-\int d\log w_-\right)=1$. For two upward branches this is the difference of angular changes $+\pi-(-\pi)=2\pi$. Reversing both branch orientations leaves the determinant sign unchanged and changes the down count by two; reversing exactly one branch reverses both the crossing sign and the factor $(-1)^{\downarrow}$. Thus under [F4] the coefficient is $+1$ for every oriented positive resolution. The localization theorem [F7] identifies this local winding contribution with the leading term of the full one-singular tangle. Thus the leading term is the one-chord diagram joining the two preimages. [F2, F4, F7, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The degree-$n$ diagram in [F7] pairs exactly the two preimages of each marked double point. Step 3.1 checks that its coefficient has sign $+1$ under the present oriented resolution convention. Local factors compose in height order, and their endpoints occur on the original circle skeleton; hence the resulting class is precisely $D$ in the unframed 4T+1T quotient. This agrees with the full principal-symbol assertion in step 2.1, including diagrams that vanish under 1T. [F1, F3, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The common factor $Z(H)^{-r}$ can be pulled outside the alternating sum because all resolutions have the same $r$. Its degree-zero coefficient is $1$, so multiplication by it preserves the first nonzero homogeneous component: the degree-$n$ component remains $D$, and all lower degrees remain zero. For $n=0$, the alternating sum is $I(K)$ and its degree-zero coefficient is $1$ by [F2]. Thus $\Delta^n I(K)=D+\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{>n}$ in every case. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume full AC for the library Jones invariant. An oriented link is a finite
disjoint union of oriented smooth circles embedded in $S^3$, considered up to
ambient isotopy; an oriented classical knot is the one-component case. For a nonempty
oriented link $L\subset S^3$, let $V_L(x)\in\mathbb Z[x^{\pm1}]$ be the
library-normalized Jones polynomial, with $V_U(x)=1$ for the unknot $U$;
write $V_K$ for its value on a knot $K$. Here $x=t^{1/2}$ in the library
convention $t=A^{-4}$, so an oriented skein triple satisfies
$$x^{-2}V_{L_+}(x)-x^2V_{L_-}(x)=(x-x^{-1})V_{L_0}(x).$$
Set $p=x-x^{-1}$. By the unique Laurent decomposition, write
$$V_K(x)=\sum_{q\ge0}(a_q(K)+b_q(K)x)p^q,$$
where $a_q(K),b_q(K)\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero. The
**Jones–Vassiliev coefficient vector of order $q$** is
$$f_q(K):=(a_q(K),b_q(K))^{\mathsf T},$$
and $c_q(K):=a_q(K)+b_q(K)$. This is the algebraic coefficient-vector
definition used by Carmi and Cohen. The claim that the coordinates of $f_q$
are finite-type invariants of order at most $q$ is a separate theorem and is
not part of this definition.

## Example

Assume full AC and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented classical knot is an
oriented smooth embedding $S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ considered up to ambient
isotopy. A regular diagram is a generic plane projection with only transverse
double points, each marked with over/under information; $c(K)$ is the least
crossing count among regular diagrams representing $K$. Let
$T=\widehat{\sigma_1^3}$ be the oriented closure of three positive two-strand
geometric half twists, with each strand oriented in the braid direction. The
figure shows the closure; its three crossings are positive under the library
determinant convention. For any classical knot $K$, let $V_K(x)$ be the
library-normalized Jones polynomial, with $V_U(x)=1$ for the unknot $U$ and
$x=t^{1/2}$ in the convention $t=A^{-4}$. Put $p=x-x^{-1}$ and write the unique finite expansion
$V_K(x)=\sum_{q\ge0}(a_q(K)+b_q(K)x)p^q$; define
$f_q(K)=(a_q(K),b_q(K))^{\mathsf T}$.

In the library Jones convention $t=A^{-4}$, the state sum gives
$V_T(t)=t+t^3-t^4$. With $x=t^{1/2}$ and $p=x-x^{-1}$, the unique
Jones–Vassiliev expansion is
$$V_T(x)=1-3p^2-4p^4-p^6+x(-6p^3-5p^5-p^7),$$
so $f_2(T)=(-3,0)^{\mathsf T}\ne0$. Carmi and Cohen's v1 preprint reports
that every nontrivial knot has such a nonzero vector at some order
$2\le q\le3c(K)$, and claims $V_K(x)=1$ implies that $K$ is the unknot.
This finite calculation checks one example only; it does not verify either
general claim or the preprint's machine-geometry proof.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$, and its closure $T$.

[F1] A state of a nonempty diagram chooses A or B at each crossing, contributes $A^{a-b}\delta^{|S|-1}$, and has $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] In the stated chart a positive braid crossing is the operator $AI+A^{-1}e_1$, where $I$ is the through pairing and $e_1$ is the cap-cup pairing ([[lem-kauffman-smoothing-operators-for-braid-crossings]]).

[F3] Closing a basis diagram identifies each top endpoint with the corresponding bottom endpoint and assigns one factor $\delta$ to each resulting circle; stacking removes each closed cycle with the same factor ([[def-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-and-partial-trace]], [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]).

[F4] The cap-cup diagram named $e_1$ in [F2] is the elementary diagram generator $d_1$, and it satisfies $d_1^2=\delta d_1$ ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], [[lem-temperley-lieb-generators-satisfy-local-relations]]).

[F5] The positive elementary half twist has endpoint permutation $(1\ 2)$, and a braid closure has one component for each cycle of its endpoint permutation ([[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]], [[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

[F6] The positive geometric Artin half twist has determinant crossing sign $+1$ ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F7] The writhe-normalized bracket of a diagram $D$ representing $K$ is $f_K(A):=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[F8] In the library convention $t=A^{-4}$, the exact Jones value of the positive trefoil closure $T=\widehat{\sigma_1^3}$ is $V_T(t)=t+t^3-t^4$ ([[def-temperley-lieb-quotient-and-jones-specialization]]).

[F9] The library Jones polynomial is an ambient-isotopy invariant and $V_U(t)=1$ ([[def-temperley-lieb-quotient-and-jones-specialization]]).

[F10] For $p=x-x^{-1}$, every Laurent Jones polynomial has a unique expansion $\sum_q(a_q+b_qx)p^q$, and $f_q=(a_q,b_q)^{\mathsf T}$ ([[def-jones-vassiliev-coefficient-vectors]], [[lem-jones-vassiliev-basis-decomposition]]).

[F11] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $c(K)$ is the least number of crossings among regular diagrams of $K$ ([[def-crossing-number-of-link]]).

[A1] Full AC supplies the library Jones-invariance hypothesis ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the countable-choice hypothesis in the crossing-number definition ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot in $S^3$ has an admissible finite planar code whose rational polygonal drawing certificate represents a regular oriented diagram of that knot.

## Statement references

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the knot can be moved off infinity and projected regularly; the projection has finitely many transverse double points and no triple points. [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F2] A finite planar code records a rational polygonal path for every edge, exact incidence and over/under data, transverse crossing vertices, and one oriented component. [[def-knot-planar-code]]

[F3] Regularity is the condition that the projected knot is an immersion with only finitely many transverse double points and no higher multiple points. [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]

[F4] An isotopy of embeddings of a compact circle extends to an ambient isotopy under AC$_\omega$. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.


1.1 Apply [F1] and list the finitely many crossings of the resulting projection. Around each crossing choose a closed disk meeting the image in exactly two transverse arcs, with all such disks pairwise disjoint. Subdivide the remaining compact arcs into finitely many subarcs contained in planar coordinate disks where each arc is a graph over a line interval and where nonincident pieces are separated. Compactness and finiteness give a positive minimum for the separations between the disjoint pieces. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 In each crossing disk, choose a nearby rational point $q$ and move the crossing there by a small planar isotopy supported in that disk. Choose two linearly independent rational direction vectors close to the two tangent directions there. Small rational multiples in both signs give four rational endpoints about $q$, in the same cyclic order as the branch germs. Replace the branches near $q$ by the two straight diameters through these endpoints, joining back inside the corresponding four disjoint sectors; this is a small isotopy of the crossing. Outside these disks, approximate each graph arc from step 1.1 by a sufficiently fine polygonal graph and perturb its finitely many vertices to rational coordinates. Choose all perturbations smaller than one third of the positive separation bound, so distinct nonincident pieces remain disjoint and every adjacent segment stays in its graph chart. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Orient the polygonal edges by the original circle parameter, pair the four crossing half-edges as on the original branches, and retain each crossing's over/under label. In each graph chart interpolate linearly between the original graph and the rational polygonal graph; the graphs remain embedded, their boundary endpoints agree, and their disjoint neighborhoods prevent new intersections. In each crossing disk the two interpolated branches keep the same four sectors and nonzero crossing determinant at the fixed rational point. Smooth each bend inside a smaller disk disjoint from all crossings. This gives an isotopy through diagrams with exactly the original crossing data. Lift the over/under heights continuously; strict height inequalities at each crossing persist, so this is an isotopy of embedded circles, which extends to an ambient isotopy by [F4]. The resulting rational polygonal data satisfy all clauses of [F2]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎
