## Statement

Assume full AC. Any two connected reduced alternating diagrams on the oriented projection sphere that represent the same oriented link type are related by a finite sequence of sphere planar isotopies and flypes. Composite links are included; the diagrams are required to be connected, and a plane drawing is interpreted as a punctured projection sphere.

## Statement references

[Menasco and Thistlethwaite, *The classification of alternating links* (1993)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2946636)

[Menasco, *Closed incompressible surfaces in alternating knot and link complements*, Theorem 1(b)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0040-9383(84)90023-5)

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, arXiv:2008.06490v3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and connected reduced alternating diagrams $D_0,D_1$ of the same oriented link type, on oriented projection spheres. Fix a smooth oriented link isotopy identifying their represented links and hence their oriented component correspondence.

[F1] A connected alternating diagram represents a nonsplit link ([[lem-connected-alternating-link-is-nonsplit]]).

[F2] A connected reduced alternating diagram realizes the crossing number of its underlying unoriented link, under countable choice, which follows here from full AC ([[thm-reduced-alternating-diagram-minimizes-crossings]]).

[F3] **Imported external prime theorem.** For reduced prime oriented alternating link diagrams and a given orientation-preserving homeomorphism of their represented oriented link pairs, the Menasco–Thistlethwaite Main Theorem gives a finite composite of flypes and flat pair maps inducing that given map's oriented component correspondence. A flat pair map is pair-isotopic to one that restricts on the projection band to $h_0\times\mathrm{id}$ for an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $h_0:S^2\to S^2$ carrying the decorated diagrams; these definitions and Theorem 2.10 are recorded in [Fontaine, §2.2, Definitions 2.8–2.9 and Theorem 2.10, pp. 11–12](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~bfontain/partiii.pdf). The imported theorem is Menasco and Thistlethwaite's [Main Theorem, p. 116](https://doi.org/10.2307/2946636) of *The classification of alternating links* (1993), not a locally reconstructed proof of its prime case. Its elementary crossing-centered flypes have the turnover convention of [[def-flype-crossing-ball-and-alternating-tangle-data]]. The published planar maps are topological; their conversion to smooth sphere planar isotopies is proved in step 6.1 below. The actual Main-Theorem statement on p. 116 was inspected, but the entire published 59-page proof is not claimed independently reverified here.

[F4] **Imported external primeness theorem.** A connected reduced alternating projection with no simple circle meeting it transversely in two ordinary points and having crossings on both sides represents a prime link, provided the represented link is nontrivial. This is the diagrammatic primeness consequence of Menasco, *Closed incompressible surfaces in alternating knot and link complements* (1984), Theorem 1(b), printed p. 37, with proof on pp. 41–42. The theorem applies to links, not only knots. It is imported here rather than reconstructed from the other normal-form research.

[F5] Given two finite decomposition-sphere systems of the same nonsplit oriented link with nontrivial prime capped factors and their reduced alternating factor diagrams, the component-marked comparison and lift applies. Its actual factor correspondences retain the oriented global component names, cap parameters, roots and boundary collars. Supplying the prime flype sequences with those induced component maps yields the original diagram sequence; no puncture-relative prime theorem is required ([[lem-component-marked-prime-decomposition-comparisons-lift-prime-flype-sequences]]).

[F6] Reducedness, alternatingness, sphere planar isotopy and flypes have the stated diagram meanings ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]], [[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]], [[def-flype-crossing-ball-and-alternating-tangle-data]]). All chosen cuts below avoid crossings and carry the strand orientations.

[F7] A smooth embedded circle on the projection sphere bounds smooth disk sides, and every orientation-preserving smooth boundary diffeomorphism between such disks extends over them with a matching collar ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]).

[F8] Every orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism of $S^2$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth isotopy through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms ([[lem-smooth-sphere-diffeomorphisms-extend-over-balls]]).

## Proof

1.1 Identify the two represented oriented links with one smooth link $L$ by the given isotopy. It is nonsplit by [F1]. Full AC supplies the choice hypotheses of [F2] and [F5]. The identification retains the actual oriented component correspondence to be used in all capped factors. [given, F1, F2, F5, construct]

1.2 In either diagram choose a smooth simple circle meeting the diagram transversely in two ordinary points whenever both sides contain crossings. By [F7] its two sides are smooth disks, so cap each cut arc by a crossing-free arc in its cap disk, carrying the endpoint pairing and orientation. Both capped shadows are connected: an additional shadow component on either side would already have been a separate component of the original shadow. Their crossing sets partition that of the piece being cut. The capped diagrams are alternating. The one proper projected arc has an even number of crossing encounters: its self-crossings contribute two visits each, and its intersections with each closed projected component are even. For the latter, decompose the closed component's finite mod-two edge set into simple cycles. Each cycle separates by [F7], and the proper arc begins and ends on the disk boundary outside those cycles, so it crosses each cycle evenly. The first and last encounters on the proper arc therefore have opposite over-under status. Closing its ends introduces no new encounter. [given, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 If $L$ is the unknot, [F2] forces both diagrams to have zero crossings. A connected crossing-free diagram is one embedded oriented circle on the projection sphere, and the two such circles are carried to one another by a sphere planar isotopy with their orientations transported. This proves the conclusion in this case. Henceforth $L$ is nontrivial and both diagrams have positive crossing count. [given, F2, F6, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 The capped diagrams are reduced. Indeed, a nugatory separator through an old crossing in a capped diagram can be moved off the crossing-free cap disk: each part in that disk lies in one of the two complementary disks of its cap arc and can be pushed to the boundary collar. It would then give a nugatory separator through the same crossing in the original piece, contrary to reducedness. The cut and caps have smooth product collars. In the represented link they are the usual twice-punctured decomposition sphere and its standard trivial-arc cap balls. [F6, F7, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Repeat these cuts in the capped pieces, retaining their cap-ball parameters and attachment collars. A later cut is moved off the interiors of earlier cap balls using their crossing-free trivial-arc product collars; equivalently shorten each artificial cap into its boundary collar before choosing the next cut. Lifting the resulting finite diagrammatic connected-sum decomposition gives pairwise disjoint decomposition spheres in the original link. Termination is finite: if a piece with $a+b$ crossings is replaced by two pieces with $a,b>0$ crossings, the sum of squared crossing counts falls by $2ab$. The final positive-crossing capped diagrams are therefore connected, reduced, alternating and have no two-point splitting circle with crossings on both sides. Crossing-free trivial connectors are suppressed while retaining all other attachment collars. [F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 Every positive-crossing terminal factor is nontrivial by [F2]; otherwise its reduced alternating crossing count would be zero. It is nonsplit by [F1] and prime by [F4]. Thus the two finite systems just constructed, with their actual cap parameters, factor diagrams and oriented component labels, satisfy exactly the decomposition hypotheses of [F5]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1]

5.1 Apply the comparison part of [F5] to those two systems in $L$. It provides the corresponding capped prime factors and actual oriented factor isotopies needed by its lift, including all refinements and suppressed trivial connectors. The correspondence transports the fixed global component names and attachment data from step 1.1. [F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 For each corresponding pair of prime factor diagrams needed in that comparison, apply the imported theorem [F3] to the orientation-preserving pair map induced by its actual capped-factor isotopy. When an intermediate topological planar map $\phi:S^2\to S^2$ carries one decorated diagram to the next, it gives a finite graph isomorphism preserving the cyclic order at every crossing, the over-under data, and the oriented strand directions. Realize that same graph isomorphism smoothly as follows. Take disjoint crossing disks and thin edge strips for the two connected projection graphs. On each crossing disk choose an orientation-preserving smooth map carrying the four branch germs to their matched germs; on each edge strip choose a smooth monotone arc map that agrees with these maps on smaller endpoint collars. The connected graph's regular neighborhood has disk complements: thicken a spanning tree to a disk, then add the other edge strips one at a time. Each new edge lies in one old disk face and cuts it along a proper arc; the two rounded boundary curves are smooth Jordan curves whose disk sides, by [F7], are exactly the two new complementary disks. By [F7] extend the matched boundary maps over these disk faces with product collars. Gluing produces an orientation-preserving smooth sphere diffeomorphism $g$ inducing exactly $\phi$'s decorated graph map and component bijection. By [F8], $g$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth orientation-preserving isotopy. Thus each topological planar map supplied by [F3] is realized by a sphere planar isotopy in the definition, with the prescribed oriented component correspondence. [F3, F6, F7, F8, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 The lift in [F5] now applies with its exact marked prime input supplied by step 6.1. It realizes the attachment transfers and prime sequences by finitely many allowed flypes and sphere planar isotopies, giving $D_0$ to $D_1$ with the fixed oriented component correspondence. Together with the crossing-free case, this proves the stated theorem for connected reduced alternating diagrams, including composite links. [F5, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

## Import and provenance limits

Facts [F3] and [F4] are explicit external inputs under the run-specific source boundary in CLAUDE §12. The proof here is the finite diagrammatic reduction and the application of the resolved marked composite supplier; it is not a local reconstruction of the published prime flyping theorem. The actual MT Main-Theorem statement on p. 116 was inspected from the supplied scan, but the entire published 59-page proof is not claimed independently reverified here. Fontaine's §2.2 statement and flat-map conventions were read as a full exposition, not as a substitute for the cited primary result. All eight actual pages of Menasco's 1984 paper, including the relevant proof, were read. Kindred's reference records the historical alternative route; none of its unresolved original-facing cap operations is used as a premise above. The finite graph realization and smooth isotopy are proved directly in step 6.1; no general topological-to-smooth equivalence theorem is imported.

## Statement refuted

Assume full AC. The positive one-crossing type-I kink of the unknot is connected and alternating but not reduced; its diagram has one crossing while the represented unknot has crossing number zero, and its normalized library Jones polynomial has $t$-span zero.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, line cap=round, line join=round]
  \draw[->,thick] (-0.22,-0.22)--(-0.045,-0.045);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.045,0.045)--(0.22,0.22);
  \draw[->,very thick] (-0.22,0.22)--(0.22,-0.22);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.22,0.22) .. controls (0.95,1.0) and (-0.95,1.0) .. (-0.22,0.22);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.22,-0.22) .. controls (0.95,-1.0) and (-0.95,-1.0) .. (-0.22,-0.22);
  \node at (0,1.25) {positive type-I kink};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The arrows orient the single component; at the central crossing, the diagonal from northwest to southeast is over and the southwest-to-northeast diagonal has a gap.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the positive type-I kink diagram $D_+$ of the unknot, and the bracket and Jones conventions in the statement.

[F1] A crossing contributes $A$ for its $A$-smoothing and $A^{-1}$ for its $B$-smoothing, a state with $k$ circles contributes $\delta^{k-1}$, and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The positive geometric crossing has sign $+1$, and writhe is the sum of crossing signs ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] A connected diagram has connected projection graph, alternation switches over-under at successive visits, and reducedness excludes a crossing repeated on a region boundary ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]]).

[F4] A type-I Reidemeister move is realized by an ambient isotopy of the represented link ([[lem-each-oriented-reidemeister-move-is-realized-by-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F5] Under full AC, the normalized bracket state sum specializes to the library Jones polynomial by $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$ with $t=A^{-4}$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[F6] The crossing number is the least crossing count among regular diagrams of the same underlying unoriented link type ([[def-crossing-number-of-link]]).

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function principle for arbitrary families of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Counterexample
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The two states of a positive kink consist of an $A$-smoothing that leaves the original arc and creates one trivial circle, and a $B$-smoothing that leaves only the original arc. By [F1] their total bracket factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=A(-A^2-A^{-2})+A^{-1}=-A^3$, so $\langle D_+\rangle=-A^3$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The kink has one positive crossing, so [F2] gives $\operatorname{wr}(D_+)=1$. Its normalized bracket is $f_{D_+}(A)=(-A^3)^{-1}(-A^3)=1$. By [A1] and [F5], the library Jones polynomial is therefore $1$, whose $t$-span is $0$. The one-crossing projection is connected; its unique component visits the crossing once over and once under, so it is alternating; the exterior region has the crossing twice on its boundary, so it is not reduced by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], the type-I move carries $D_+$ to the crossing-free unknot diagram. Thus the represented link has a diagram with zero crossings. Since crossing counts are nonnegative by [F6], its crossing number is zero, strictly less than the one crossing in $D_+$. This verifies the claimed failure of crossing minimality at a non-reduced alternating diagram. [F4, F6, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

kind: lemma
title: Positive-Euler finite PL surfaces are disks, spheres or projective planes
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

        (1961),245–375

      locator: Chapter5, printed pp.360–374, positive-Euler summands in the
        fundamental-surface argument. The small finite surface classification
        used here is proved below.

## Statement

Let $P$ be a connected compact surface supplied with a finite PL triangulation. The following conclusions require no choice axiom.

1. If $\partial P\ne\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le1$. Equality holds only for a disk. If instead $\chi(P)=0$, then $P$ is an annulus or a Mobius band; these have respectively two and one boundary circles.
2. If $\partial P=\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P$ is a two-sphere; if $\chi(P)=1$, then $P$ is a projective plane.

Consequently, every positive-Euler connected finite PL surface is a disk, sphere or projective plane. These identifications can be made by PL homeomorphisms between finite polygonal models. In a PL three-manifold without an embedded projective plane, a connected embedded positive-Euler surface is therefore a disk or a sphere.

## Statement references

[[def-finite-triangulated-compact-surface]] — the supplied finite triangulation.

[[ex-cylinder-and-mobius-band-as-quotients]] — the annular and twisted rectangular-band models.

[[ex-projective-plane-polygonal-schema]] — the antipodal-boundary disk model of the projective plane.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite triangulation of the connected compact surface $P$.

[F1] [[def-simplicial-euler-characteristic]]: $\chi=V-E+F$. An elementary collapse of a triangle and a free edge removes one face and one edge, preserving this number. Attaching a disk along a subdivided circle adds one, because the circle has equally many vertices and edges.

[F2] The dual spanning-tree collapse in [[lem-connected-normal-surface-chi-one-is-disk]], steps 1.1–2.1, applies to any connected finite triangulated surface with boundary, without using its Euler characteristic: it leaves a connected graph. Its step 4.1 proves the tree-neighborhood case. The graph-neighborhood construction for the general case is detailed below.

[F3] [[ex-cylinder-and-mobius-band-as-quotients]] specifies the two rectangle quotients $(0,y)\sim(1,y)$ and $(0,y)\sim(1,1-y)$. [[ex-projective-plane-polygonal-schema]] identifies a disk with antipodal boundary points paired as a projective plane, by an explicit finite quotient argument.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose first that $P$ has boundary. Apply the finite dual-tree collapse [F2], choosing a lexicographically first spanning tree, to obtain a connected graph $G$. Take small polygonal vertex disks and narrow rectangular edge bands inside $P$ to form a regular neighborhood $N(G)$. One can choose them after a finite subdivision by taking sufficiently small rational distances in the finitely many triangle charts. Reversing a free triangle-edge collapse enlarges this neighborhood by a boundary finger across that triangle. To see that its homeomorphism type is unchanged, use a triangle chart in which the removed edge is the base: the two retained sides make the tip of the finger, and moving its polygonal boundary from a small parallel arc to the base expands a disk along one boundary interval. Triangulate the region between these two arcs and map corresponding triangles linearly. This gives a PL homeomorphism between the two neighborhoods, fixed off that triangle and its small vertex sectors. Reverse the finitely many collapses in order and finally expand the boundary collar. Thus $P$ is PL homeomorphic to $N(G)$. This construction uses a finite list of local maps, rather than a general regular-neighborhood uniqueness theorem. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 A spanning tree of the connected graph $G$ has $V(G)-1$ edges. Write $h=E(G)-V(G)+1\ge0$ for the number of remaining edges. The collapses and [F1] give $\chi(P)=V(G)-E(G)=1-h\le1$. If equality holds, $h=0$, so $G$ is a tree and its neighborhood is a disk by [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\chi(P)=0$, the graph $G$ has exactly one edge outside a spanning tree. Delete its leaf edges successively. A leaf vertex disk and its band merely form a finger on the neighboring disk; removing that finger changes no neighborhood homeomorphism type by the same finite polygonal expansion as in step 1.1. The graph remaining is one cycle: alternatively, the unique extra edge and the unique tree path joining its endpoints form that cycle, and every other tree edge belongs to a tree attached to it. Thus $N(G)$ is the union of the vertex disks and bands around a single cycle. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 Now suppose $P$ is closed. Remove the interior of a small polygonal disk $B$ inside one triangle and triangulate the remaining surface $P_0$. It is connected: any path crossing the disk can have each crossing segment replaced by a path along its boundary, and a finite polygonal path has only finitely many such segments after a small general-position displacement. It has exactly one boundary circle. By [F1], $\chi(P_0)=\chi(P)-1$, and step 2.1 gives $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P_0$ is a disk by step 2.1. Capping a disk by a disk gives a sphere. Any PL boundary identification can be reduced to the identity by extending the boundary map over a disk: cone a finite subdivision of its circle to the center, and map the resulting triangles linearly. Thus this identification is PL. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Cut this cycle across one band. Its neighborhood becomes one rectangular strip: glue the remaining vertex disks and bands consecutively, each along one boundary interval, and use the polygonal disk expansions of step 1.1 to straighten the strip. At its two ends the transverse intervals are identified by a PL interval homeomorphism. If this map is increasing, change the transverse coordinate at one end and interpolate that change along the strip to make the gluing the identity. Explicitly, prescribe the required increasing map on one short side of the rectangle and the identity on its other three sides. This is a PL homeomorphism of its boundary. Subdivide at its finitely many breakpoints, cone both boundary subdivisions to interior points and map corresponding triangles linearly. This extends the boundary map to a PL homeomorphism of the rectangle. If the gluing is decreasing, first compose with $y\mapsto1-y$ and apply the same construction. The two resulting quotients are exactly the two models in [F3]. In the first, the two long sides of the strip give two boundary circles; in the second they join to one. Hence $P$ is respectively an annulus or a Mobius band. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 If $\chi(P)=1$, then $P_0$ has Euler characteristic zero and exactly one boundary circle. Steps 3.1–4.1 make it a Mobius band, since the annulus has two boundary circles. ## Statement

For every valid connected one-component oriented planar knot code with $n$ crossings together with a specified polygonal realization $P$ whose regular projection has that code, there is an explicit finite combinatorial construction of a triangulated $S^3$ containing that same $P$ as a subcomplex. An abstract valid code can first be realized by the stated reconstruction procedure and then used as $P$. A **good exterior triangulation** is the triangulation inherited on the complement of the interior of a regular neighborhood made from one fixed ball around each vertex of $P$ and one fixed tube block along each edge, with its boundary torus triangulated and a meridian path marked. The construction gives a good exterior triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra for one universal constant $C$, and the marked meridian is a path of at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges. At $n=0$ the construction uses a fixed solid-torus exterior triangulation.

A local crossing is lifted by separating the over- and under-strands in the interval direction; the schematic below records only the projected crossing, with the continuous strand passing over the gapped strand.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.15]
\draw[very thick] (-1,-1)--(1,1);
\draw[thick] (-1,1)--(-0.18,0.18);
\draw[thick] (0.18,-0.18)--(1,-1);
\node at (0.62,0.78) {over};
\node at (-0.70,0.76) {under};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The picture records only the planar local incidence. The proof constructs disjoint arcs in a three-dimensional crossing block and does not infer embeddedness from the drawing.

## Statement references

[[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]] — dart, crossing, orientation, and face-cycle conventions.

[[lem-planar-diagram-code-realizability-and-face-validation]] — a valid spherical rotation system has a polygonal realization with disk faces.

[[alg-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction]] — the finite crossing-disk, edge-band and face-cap gluing record.

[[thm-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction-procedure-properties]] — the reconstruction record represents the declared oriented diagram.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, §7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — linear-size triangulation of a knot exterior from a diagram.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid connected one-component oriented planar knot code with $n$ crossings and a specified polygonal realization $P$ of that code.

[F1] [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]: the code gives a finite connected four-valent graph, directed strand pairings, over/under data and a face permutation.

[F2] [[lem-planar-diagram-code-realizability-and-face-validation]]: when $V-E+F=2$, the rotation system has a spherical polygonal realization with disk faces.

[F3] [[alg-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction]]: a passing code yields one crossing disk per crossing, one edge band per edge, and one cap per face, with recorded ports and face cycles.

[F4] [[thm-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction-procedure-properties]]: the output gluing record represents the oriented link diagram described by the input code.

## Proof

1.1 If $n>0$, there are $4n$ darts and $2n$ paired edges. The connected crossing graph has $V=n$, $E=2n$, and hence $F=2-V+E=n+2$ faces by [F2]. The sum of face-boundary port occurrences, counted with multiplicity, is $2E=4n$. Choose disjoint small disks around the graph vertices and disjoint narrow rectangular bands along its edges, attached in the prescribed cyclic order. Their union $N(G)$ is a connected planar subsurface of the sphere; each boundary component is one face cycle, and the closure of each complementary component is a disk. The total number of vertex-disk ports, band sides and boundary occurrences is bounded by a universal constant times $n$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Triangulate each vertex disk and edge band by fixed templates. Subdivide every side occurrence on each complementary face boundary circle by a fixed number of new vertices and cone the resulting simple polygon to one interior vertex. Each face of boundary length $d$ contributes at most $c_0d$ triangles for a fixed $c_0$, and $\sum d=O(n)$ by step 1.1. Since the face boundary circles of $N(G)$ are embedded circles with port occurrences kept distinct, these are regular disk triangulations; matching subdivisions along shared ports and one fixed barycentric subdivision give a genuine finite simplicial triangulation of the projection sphere with $O(n)$ triangles. [step 1.1, F3, construct]

3.1 Take the product of this triangulated sphere with an interval. Each triangular prism is split into three tetrahedra by the fixed staircase subdivision; cap the two ends by coning their triangulated boundary spheres to obtain a triangulated $S^3$ with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. In each crossing disk, place the over- and under-strand arcs at distinct interval heights and connect each pair of opposite ports; along each edge band connect its end ports by a linear arc whose height interpolates between the endpoint heights. In a crossing block the two arcs are disjoint because their heights differ; interiors of distinct edge blocks are disjoint, and every edge arc joins only its designated crossing ports. A fixed subdivision of each crossing and edge block makes these finitely many local arc templates subcomplexes. For the supplied $P$, choose the disks and bands along its actual projection. Carry the templates to its actual strand heights by increasing piecewise-linear maps of the interval fibres, fixed at the top and bottom; at a crossing the prescribed two heights have the same order, so both can be matched. Choose the maps identically on shared port collars and extend over the remaining face regions, triangulating the finitely many height graphs and interpolating between successive levels. Extend over the two end balls by coning the boundary maps. These maps give a PL homeomorphism of the template sphere carrying its template knot to the supplied $P$. Transport the triangulation through it. Its abstract simplex count remains $O(n)$, even if the PL parametrizations require further subdivisions in ambient coordinates; thus the same $P$ is a subcomplex. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Around each vertex and edge of the 1-subcomplex $P$, take the fixed ball and tube blocks from the definition of a good exterior triangulation. Choose a normal 2-frame at one point, extend it across the finitely many edge and vertex blocks, and adjust the final frame along the last edge by a path of rotations in $SO(2)$ to agree with the initial frame. Thus their union is the product $S^1\times D^2$, a solid torus with triangulated boundary. The number of blocks and tetrahedra per block is constant, so removing its interior leaves a compact triangulated exterior with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. At an interior point of a chosen knot edge, the fixed local tube template has a meridian circle using a fixed number of boundary edges; mark that path. [step 3.1, F4, construct]

5.1 If $n=0$, use the standard genus-one product decomposition of $S^3$ into two solid tori and the fixed product triangulation of the exterior solid torus as a triangle times a three-edge circle. Splitting its three triangular prisms into three tetrahedra each and marking the three-edge circle $\{a_0\}\times S^1$ on its boundary gives a fixed-size model: this is the original knot's meridian, meeting an exterior disk boundary once. For a supplied crossingless $P$, parametrize its polygonal projection disk and the complementary sphere disk and match its height graph by the same fibre construction as in step 3.1; transport the fixed model through the resulting PL homeomorphism. Increasing $C$ to dominate this model and all fixed local template constants in steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 yields both stated $C(n+1)$ bounds. All code-dependent choices use the finite label and port order, so the construction is explicit. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Whenever the JT branch of the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson search returns a disk-certificate, its primitive vertex normal surface is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in the triangulated knot exterior.

## Statement references

[[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]] — JT primitive-ray enumeration and candidate tests.

[[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]] — exact disk and essential-boundary characterization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid one-component knot code and a primitive ray vector returned by the JT branch as a disk-certificate.

[F1] [[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]]: a returned JT vector is primitive on an extreme ray, admissible, and passes the nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic-one and odd-meridian-intersection tests.

[F2] [[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]]: a fundamental normal surface is connected.

[F3] [[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]]: a connected admissible normal surface passing the nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic-one and odd-meridian tests is a properly embedded disk with essential boundary.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the returned vector is admissible and is the primitive integer generator of an extreme ray. If it split into two nonzero admissible integer vectors, both summands would lie on that same extreme ray; primitivity forbids such a positive integral split. Hence the vector is fundamental, and [F2] makes its surface connected. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The remaining tests checked by [F1], together with [F3], identify the connected surface as a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $f(M,L)$, its Newton polygon is the convex hull in $\mathbb R^2$ of exponent pairs $(a,b)$ for which the coefficient of $M^bL^a$ is nonzero. Then the enhanced A-polynomial of $K$ is thin if and only if $K$ is a torus knot, including the unknot.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $a\ge b\ge1$ be coprime positive integers, and let $T_{a,b}\subset S^3$ be the corresponding torus knot. If a knot $K\subset S^3$ has the same enhanced A-polynomial as $T_{a,b}$ up to a Laurent unit and the same Alexander-polynomial breadth (highest exponent minus lowest exponent of its symmetrized Alexander polynomial), then $K$ has the same underlying unoriented knot type as $T_{a,b}$. When $b\ge2$, the absolute torus parameters of $K$ agree with $\{a,b\}$.

## Statement references

[[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots|Thin enhanced-A classification]]

[[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas|Alexander breadth formula for torus knots]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Corollary 1.4 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a knot $K$, a positive torus knot $T_{a,b}$, equality of enhanced A-polynomials up to a Laurent unit, and equality of Alexander breadths.

[F1] A knot whose enhanced A-polynomial has Newton polygon contained in a line is a torus knot. For a positive nontrivial torus knot $T_{a,b}$ with $a>b\ge2$, its enhanced A-polynomial has a line-segment Newton polygon of slope $ab$ in the stated convention; the unknot has enhanced A-polynomial $1$ ([[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots]]; [[lem-torus-knot-enhanced-a-polynomial]]). The same segment-slope formula holds for signed parameters: the mirror changes peripheral coordinates by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L)$, reversing the knot orientation changes them by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L^{-1})$, and these transformations are proved for the enhanced locus in [[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots]], Proof2.1. They send the positive segment slope $|pq|$ to the signed product $pq$.

[F2] For signed coprime parameters, the Alexander breadth of $T_{p,q}$ is $(|p|-1)(|q|-1)$; changing both signs reverses knot orientation and changing one sign takes the mirror ([[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas]]; [[def-coprime-torus-knot]]).

[F3] A torus knot with one parameter of absolute value $1$ is the standard unknot ([[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot]]).

[A1] Full AC implies countable choice, the hypothesis used by [F3] ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F4] The classification used in [F1] is now complete with the explicit external input Baldwin–Sivek, arXiv:2405.19197v2, Theorem 1.2. Their Corollary 1.4 (p.2) independently states detection by the enhanced polynomial together with Alexander degree; the finite parameter-recovery proof below is retained locally. The source statement was consulted directly, not its gauge-theoretic proof reconstructed. The breadth used here is twice the degree of the symmetric polynomial for torus knots, so equality of breadths gives exactly the equality used in step2.1.

## Proof

1.1 Equality of enhanced A-polynomials up to a Laurent unit gives the same Newton polygon shape. By [F1], this polygon lies in a line, so write $K=T_{p,q}$ for signed coprime nonzero parameters. If $b\ge2$, both polygons are line segments and [F1] gives equality of slopes, hence $pq=ab$. If $b=1$, the target polygon is a point and no slope equation is asserted. [F1, given, cases, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $b\ge2$ and put $u=|p|$, $v=|q|$. From $pq=ab>0$, $p$ and $q$ have the same sign and $uv=ab$. Equality of Alexander breadths and [F2] give $(u-1)(v-1)=(a-1)(b-1)$. Expanding and substituting $uv=ab$ yields $u+v=a+b$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $b=1$. Then [F3] says $T_{a,1}$ is the unknot, whose Alexander breadth is zero. By [F2] and the assumed breadth equality, $(|p|-1)(|q|-1)=0$. Thus $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3], so $K=T_{p,q}$ is the unknot as well. Hence its underlying unoriented knot type equals $T_{a,1}$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The monic quadratics $x^2-(u+v)x+uv$ and $x^2-(a+b)x+ab$ are equal, so their root multisets agree and $\{u,v\}=\{a,b\}$. The same-sign conclusion in step 2.1 means that $K$ is $T_{a,b}$ up to orientation, so the underlying unoriented knot types agree. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 2.2 cover respectively the nontrivial and unknot target cases, proving the stated identification; in the nontrivial case step 3.1 also identifies the absolute parameters up to interchange. [step 3.1, step 2.2] ∎
